# Removing the Cigar Lighter Socket in the Outback Load Area

If you are attempting to charge a LiFePO4 battery using the auxiliary power outlet in your 2022 Subaru Outback, you have likely encountered a classic automotive electrical issue: severe voltage drop. You correctly identified that while the factory fuse is rated for 20A, the circuit design and internal wiring typically limit safe operation to 10A to prevent melting the plastic socket housing. Even if your external charger has current limiting logic set to 10A, the physics of the connection remain unchanged.

When you measure 9V at the plug under load instead of the expected 12V+, and observe the positive terminal heating up significantly, you are witnessing resistive heating in action ($P = I^2R$). That heat is dangerous not just to the socket housing, but potentially to the surrounding trim and wiring harness. The solution is to bypass the high-resistance soldered joint inside the factory socket entirely by replacing the assembly with a robust Anderson Power Pole connector.

The primary mechanical hurdle here is accessing the retention mechanism without destroying the interior trim or the hatch itself. In most Subaru models, including the Outback, the load area socket is not retained by screws but by friction-fit clips designed to snap into the plastic tunnel. The access hatch you see in your photo is simply a cover plate; it does not mechanically secure the socket assembly.

To remove the unit, you need to apply steady upward pressure directly on the socket face while pulling it outward from the rear of the trim panel. Do not pry against the surrounding trim rails or the hatch cover, as this will crack the brittle ABS plastic common in older automotive interiors. Once the socket pops free, inspect the wiring harness connector at the base. It is usually a standard Subaru 2-pin or multi-pin connector that can be released by pressing the locking tab and pulling straight back.

Replacing the socket with an Anderson connector offers two distinct advantages: superior current handling and a much lower resistance interface. The factory socket relies on spring tension against a small metal pin, which degrades over time and creates high resistance points. An Anderson connector provides a positive latch mechanism and a larger contact surface area, virtually eliminating the voltage drop issue you are experiencing.

However, there are critical implementation details to consider before cutting into your vehicle's wiring. You must match the gauge of the existing wires to the new connector. The factory wiring for this auxiliary circuit is likely 18AWG or 20AWG. If you install a heavy-duty Anderson connector (e.g., Series 4), you will be limited by the wire gauge unless you run a new, heavier-gauge cable from the battery to the load area. Running a dedicated high-current cable from the main battery in the trunk or under the hood is often the safest approach, ensuring that the only current path is through thick copper and not thin automotive wiring.

Regarding your observations about the purple component with the "K" logo near the fuel filler: this is likely part of the fuel vapor venting system or a specific OEM cable routing guide, unrelated to the electrical circuit. Since the cord heads toward the fuel filler, it may be shielding or grounding wire associated with that area, but it does not interfere with removing the load socket.

When installing the Anderson connector, ensure you use an inline fuse holder rated for your new wire gauge and place it as close to the power source as possible. If you are using the existing factory fuse (20A), remember that the Anderson connector itself can handle much more current, so your safety device remains the limiting factor. This setup allows you to safely charge your LiFePO4 battery without risking damage to the vehicle's interior or creating a fire hazard from overheated contacts.
